titulo: Sounds, alphabet and first words: Reading French: accents, silent letters and liaison

aula.objetivo: Spell in French, recognize the sounds that English does not have (u, eu, nasal vowels, r), understand silent letters, liaison and elision, and say your first greetings.

sessao.titulo: Reading French: accents, silent letters and liaison

blocos.contexto: Emma goes into a café and orders a coffee from the waiter. Listen carefully for the letters that are not pronounced and for the liaisons.

linhas.en: — Good morning, madam! How are you?

linhas.ru: — Ça va bien, merci. Un café, s'il vous plaît.
linhas.en: — Fine, thank you. A coffee, please.
linhas.audio: Ça va bien, merci. Un café, s'il vous plaît.

linhas.en: — You're welcome. Have a good day, madam!

linhas.ru: — Pardon, monsieur... Un café, c'est bon ?
linhas.en: — Excuse me, sir... Is the coffee good?
linhas.audio: Pardon, monsieur... Un café, c'est bon ?

linhas.en: — Yes, madam, it is very good!

blocos.explicacao: Listen first: «café», «père», «garçon», «petit», «bonjour». STEP 1: the acute accent, «é», gives a closed «ay» sound: «café», «été». STEP 2: the grave accent, «è», and the circumflex, «ê», give an open «eh» sound: «père», «mère», «fête». STEP 3: the circumflex on «â», «î», «ô» and «û» almost always just shows that an old letter has disappeared. It does not change the sound much: «hôtel», «bientôt». STEP 4: the cedilla, «ç», always sounds like «s»: «garçon», «français», «ça». STEP 5: most consonants at the end of a word are silent: «petit», «grand», «vous», «trop», «bon». STEP 6: the consonants «c», «r», «f» and «l» are often pronounced at the end. Remember the English word «careful»: «sac», «bonjour», «chef», «animal».
blocos.comparacao: English spelling is famously irregular, but French has its own system: many letters at the end of words are silent. The first question when you see a French word is: what do I hear? Not: what do I read?

erros.motivo: A final consonant is usually silent.
The «ç» sounds like «s»; without the cedilla, the «c» would sound like «k».

erros.errado: saying «café» with an open last syllable
erros.motivo: The acute accent gives a closed «ay» sound.

blocos.titulo: Liaison and elision: words join together
blocos.explicacao: Listen first: «les amis», «vous avez», «j'aime», «l'ami». STEP 1: «liaison» (linking) happens when the next word begins with a vowel. The final consonant, which was silent, is now pronounced, linked to the vowel. STEP 2: the liaison «s» sounds like «z». «Les amis» sounds like «lay-zah-MEE». «Vous avez» sounds like «voo-zah-VAY». STEP 3: elision cuts the final vowel of short words before a vowel. In its place we write an apostrophe. «Je» plus «aime» becomes «j'aime». «Le» plus «ami» becomes «l'ami». «Ce» plus «est» becomes «c'est». STEP 4: say the sentence like a continuous wave, with no pauses between words. «J'aime le café» sounds almost like one word.
blocos.comparacao: English also runs words together: «give it up» sounds like «gi-vi-TUP». In French this is a mandatory rule: elision even shows up in writing, with the apostrophe.

tabela.examples: les amis, vous avez, ils ont

erros.motivo: The «s» links to the vowel and sounds like «z».

itens.explicacao: Listen to the beginning: «un» has the nasal «an». «Du» has the «ew» and «le» has the weak «e».
Listen to the «s» of «ç» and the final nasal «ohn».
The expression has two parts: «bonne» and «journée».
Write: un café. The acute accent is on the final «e».

itens.enunciado: Which letter has the sound of a closed «ay»?
itens.explicacao: The acute accent gives the closed «ay», as in «café».

itens.enunciado: In «petit», what happens to the final «t»?
itens.explicacao: Most final consonants are silent: «petit» is said without the final t.
It is the standard order in any café in France.

blocos.enunciado: Act out the dialogue «Au café» aloud, playing both voices. Watch out: «un café» (an ka-FAY), «s'il vous plaît» and «c'est très bon» linked, with no pauses.
Say aloud: tu, rue, bon, deux, pain. What is the sound of each one? Which of them has the nasal vowel «an»?
